headline: Barry Dawes is bearish on gold, targeting a pullback to $3,500 and potentially $2,700, citing parabolic exhaustion and structural oversupply via ETFs
reasoning: Dawes notes that gold's parabolic rise produced gaps with no consolidation, meaning there is no support built into the structure on the way down. He argues annual supply of approximately 5,000 tonnes requires strong ETF buying of around 1,400 tonnes to balance the market, but that demand is not materialising. Jewellery demand has collapsed and central banks, despite rhetoric, are not buying meaningfully. Western retail demand for bars and coins has been very weak. He sees a 4,000-tonne overhang in ETFs sitting on massive unrealised profits as a significant downside risk, with a target of $3,500 and a reasonable probability of $2,700.
quote: I'm a bear on gold. I was a bit premature in getting very late last year, but I think when we'd seen the parabolic moves and the breaches of all those parabolas and the downward... the character of parabolas when they run up like that is that they don't generate any support. Each move, often the moves were gaps higher and there was no consolidation. Everyone was wildly bullish. Consequently, there's now no support. So I think we're going to see ourselves back to 3500. And I think probably there's a reasonable probability we're going to see back around 2700... that 4000 tonnes overhang in the ETFs, I think will be disastrous for gold. And you've got 200 and 220,000 tonnes of previously mined gold just sitting there sitting on the biggest profit in any market at any time.
episode_title: Barry's lighting the fuse on energy stocks

headline: Barry Dawes suggests smaller gold stocks that missed the rally can still be played as growth stories where resource discovery matters more than spot price
reasoning: Dawes notes that many smaller gold stocks did not participate in the large gold price rally of the past year, which means they did not become overvalued relative to the spot price move. He argues that for these companies, discovering significant resources such as a million-ounce deposit remains a value-creating event regardless of whether gold is at $3,500 or $4,000. Resource growth is the primary driver of value for these names, making them viable as growth stock investments even in a falling gold price environment.
quote: A lot of the smaller gold stocks just didn't participate in the big rally last year. And so I like to think of those as growth stocks and where they have resource growth, that's not really going to matter if it's 3500 USD or 4000 USD. If you find 1,000,000 ounce deposit. So I think you can still play those sorts of games.
episode_title: Barry's lighting the fuse on energy stocks

headline: Barry Dawes calls Amiga's work in the Taroom Trough a game changer for Australian tight gas with liquids upside

headline: Barry Dawes bullish on oil prices, expects significantly higher levels driven by product tightness and resumption of Chinese imports
reasoning: Dawes had previously expected oil to fall below $60/barrel due to Venezuela supply and hoped the Iran conflict would be resolved, but markets have not confirmed that view. He notes a technical breakout and back-test of the breakout line followed by a bounce. Across oil products he sees tightness, with gasoline and other products not falling even as crude softened. A massive drawdown of approximately 900 billion barrels has occurred across markets. China paused imports due to its own large stockpile, suppressing price pressure, but that is now changing. He expects much higher oil prices ahead.
quote: I thought we were going to get the oil price back under $60 a barrel because of the changes in the world outlook with Venezuela coming in. And hopefully that the Iran conflict would have been over by now, but that hasn't happened. And so we've got to heed the markets... right across the range of oil products we've got tightness. So the oil price itself might have come down, but the gasoline price didn't... there's been a massive drawdown of probably 900 billion barrels... the only reason that the oil price didn't go a lot higher was the fact that China stopped importing... Now that's changing. And I think we're going to see much higher oil prices here.
